sections.heading: Abstract
sections.text: Electromechanical energy demands on homogenous thick films of piezoceramics with sufficiently large piezoelectric constant and reproducible performance. Singlephase $\mathrm { L i T a O } _ { 3 }$ films deposited by sol-gel processing have been fabricated as cantilevers to investigate the interdependence of dielectric and piezoelectric properties as a function of film thickness. Phase pure $\mathrm { L i T a O } _ { 3 }$ films with varying thickness in the range of $2 . 0 7 { - } 4 . 3 7 ~ \mu \mathrm { m }$ on stainless steel substrates were obtained after calcination of samples at $6 5 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ . The relative permittivity of optimized spin-coated films peaked at 479.73 $\mathrm { { ( 1 ~ k H z ) } }$ ), whereas the piezoelectric coefficient $\mathrm { \Delta } \mathrm { \hat { d } } _ { 3 3 }$ mode) determined by piezoresponse force microscopy was in the range of $2 1 { - } 2 4 \mathrm { p m } / \mathrm { V }$ . The effect of poling was studied through the butterfly and phase curves. A figure of merit (FOM) up to 3.29 $( 1 0 ^ { - 1 8 } \mathrm m ^ { 2 } / \mathrm V ^ { 2 } )$ was determined for cantilever devices, which were able to generate a peak-to-peak voltage of $0 . 0 4 6 \substack { - 0 . 1 5 \mathrm { ~ V ~ } }$ using a $1 \ \mathbf { M } \Omega$ resistor as an impedance load at a fixed acceleration of $1 . 5 ~ \mathrm { m / s } ^ { 2 }$ . While the power density was in the range of ${ \sim } 4 { - } 2 0 \times 1 0 ^ { - 9 } \mathrm { W / m } ^ { 3 }$ , which increased with the increasing film thickness. The leakage current density decreased in the range of $4 \times 1 0 ^ { - 5 } { \mathrm { - } } 6 \times 1 0 ^ { - 7 } { \mathrm { A / m } } ^ { 2 }$ in the same direction. As both ferroelectric and piezoelectric properties of $\mathrm { L i T a O } _ { 3 }$ films are dependent on film thickness, an optimal energy conversion efficiency was obtained for a thickness of ${ \sim } 3 ~ { \mu \mathrm { m } }$ . Furthermore, these devices were tested up to a temperature of $1 5 0 \mathrm { { } ^ { \circ } C }$ for voltage generation. Given the need for lead-free piezoelectric materials for environmental applications, these $\mathrm { L i T a O } _ { 3 }$ cantilevers are very promising for vibrational energy harvester (VEH) applications especially due to their cost effectiveness, small size, stability at higher temperatures, and repeatable properties, which makes them suitable for MEMS devices for industrial applications.

sections.heading: KEYWORDS
sections.text: $\mathrm { L i T a O } _ { 3 }$ , perovskite, piezoceramics, thick films, vibrational energy harvesters

sections.heading: 1 | INTRODUCTION
sections.text:
Energy harvesting piezoelectric ceramics are ideal power sources for wireless sensor networks and already small piezoelements of few $\mathrm { m m } ^ { 2 }$ sizes can replace a battery system to run autonomous microsystem.' Piezoelectric materials with high electromechanical coupling can directly convert mechanical vibrations into electrical energy. Lithium tantalate $\left( \mathrm { L i T a O } _ { 3 } \right)$ is a perovskite compound with high Curie temperature $\mathrm { \mathit { T } _ { c } } = 6 5 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } )$ and can be thus used at elevated temperatures for electromechanical energy harvesting, for instance, in high-temperature acoustic transducer.2 Given its wide transparency range $( \lambda = 4 0 0 – 5 0 0 \ \mathrm { n m } )$ , $\mathrm { L i T a O } _ { 3 }$ has found its applications in surface acoustic wave (SAW) and photonic devices.3 Despite its promising properties, the us of $\mathrm { L i T a O } _ { 3 }$ remains scarce, mainly due to its lower piezoelectric coefficient when compared to other lead-free alternatives such as potassium sodium niobate (KNN).4

$\mathrm { L i T a O } _ { 3 }$ has been synthesized by thermal evaporation,5 pyrosol process,6 magnetron sputtering,7 chemical vapor deposition, laser ablation,and molecular beam epi.1 Although the films deposited by gas-phase techniques show good adherence to the substrate, precise and reproducible control over the stoichiometric composition is a persisting challenge that limits industrial applications. In this context, sol-gel processing based on the coating of a molecularly engineered sol is a promising technique to control both microand macroscopic homogeneity of sample composition. The covalent cross-linking of the cationic centers in sol (-[-(OR)- Ta-(OR)(OH)(O)-Li-(OR)-]-) inhibits phase segregation into Li and Ta oxides commonly observed in other fabrication methods. In addition, films prepared by spin coating of a sol enable reproducible control over film thickness as recently shown for KNN films.11

Many ceramics and polymers exhibit piezoelectric properties, which allows the direct conversion between mechanical and electrical energy. Hereby, lead zirconate titanate (PZT, $\mathrm { P b } [ \mathrm { Z r _ { x } T i _ { 1 - x } } ] \mathrm { O } _ { 3 } )$ has the most promising piezoelectric properties mainly due to its high electromechanical coupling coef-However, as a lead-containing compound, its commercial application is restricted to piezoelectric devices currently approved until 2021 in the European Union and not having any sitable replacement alternatives. $^ { 1 4 } \mathrm { L i T a O } _ { 3 }$ is a potential contender for lead-free piezoelectric materials; however, due to its low piezoelectric coefficients (typically $\mathrm { d } _ { 3 3 } = 2 1 \mathrm { p m } / \mathrm { V } ,$ $\mathrm { d } _ { 1 5 } = 2 6 ~ \mathrm { p m } / \mathrm { V } ) ^ { 1 5 - 1 7 }$ this material is less studied when compared to other lead-free alternatives such as KNN (typically d33 = 80 pm/V).18,19

Vibrational energy harvesters (VEHs) can be used to run low-power devices, such as watches, microphones, sensors, harvesting can be realized by integrating piezoelectric materials in different geometries, using different methods. For example, a circular diaphragm array,22 piezo fiber composites,23 low-frequency piezo QuickPack,24 three-axis energy harvester,25 bistable energy harvesters with a synchronized switch harvester on inductor (SSHI) circuit,26 and bulk micromachined energy harvesters.2 However, applying current fabrication techniques, Microelectromechanical systems (MEMS)-based techniques often require complex multi-step processing, which leads to the manufacturing cost remains high. $^ { 2 8 } \mathrm { L i T a O } _ { 3 }$ -based devices could be an ideal choice for energy harvesting in a high-temperature environment $\mathrm { < } 7 2 3 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } )$ . Owing to the low voltage generated by piezoelectric materials, they are mostly used in pressure and displacement transducers, and to power up the sensors. Moreover, due to their small size, they are compact and easy-to-use devices.29

The sol-gel technique involves shrinkage risk and film cracks can appear due to repetitive layer deposition.30 For VEH applications, a thicker film is desired.31 We report here, reproducible solution-based processing of $\mathrm { L i T a O } _ { 3 }$ films with a controllable thickness (Figure 1). Compared to other piezoelectric ceramics (e.g., PZT, $( \mathrm { K } , \mathrm { N a } ) \mathrm { N b } { \mathrm { O } } _ { 3 }$ , and $\mathrm { L i N b O } _ { 3 } ,$ , $\mathrm { L i T a O } _ { 3 }$ is studied to a lesser extent mainly due to synthetic challenges associated with phase purity and stoichiometric variability. The approach chosen in this work enables reproducible control over film stoichiometry and grain uniformity leading to a sufficiently high piezoelectric coefficient (approx. $\mathrm { d } _ { 3 3 } = 2 1 { - } 2 4 ~ \mathrm { p m } / \mathrm { V } )$ and good reproducibility.

sections.heading: 2 | MATERIALS AND METHODS
sections.text:
$\mathrm { L i T a O } _ { 3 }$ was synthesized following a sol-gel approach using a stoichiometric mixture of $\mathrm { L i O } ^ { \mathrm { t } } \mathrm { B u } ^ { 3 2 }$ and $[ \mathrm { T a ( O E t ) } _ { 5 } ] _ { 2 }$ b $9 9 . 9 9 \%$ pure, abcr GmbH, CAS: 6074-84-6) dissolved in 2-propanol $( 9 9 . 9 \%$ pure, Sigma Aldrich, CAS: 67-63-0). Glacial acetic acid was added as a chelating agent to the solution of alkoxides and the resulting mixture was stirred for $^ { 5 \mathrm { h } }$ at $4 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for hydrolysis, forming a $0 . 7 { } \mathrm { ~ M ~ }$ sol. Further, ethyl cellulose (toluene/ethanol 80:20(lit); $4 8 \%$ ethoxyl, Sigma Aldrich, CAS: 9004-57-3) was added and the solution was stirred for $1 5 \mathrm { h }$ to make the sol more viscous. Before performing the spin coating, the sol was filtered using a $2 \mu \mathrm { m }$ filter.

The resulting sol was spin-coated (1680 rpm) on stainless steel $( \mathrm { F e } / \mathrm { C r } 1 5 / \mathrm { N i } 7 / \mathrm { M o } 2 . 2 5 )$ substrates $( 1 8 \times 1 8 \times 0 . 1 2 5 ~ \mathrm { m m } ^ { 3 } )$ with subsequent heating at $5 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for $1 5 \mathrm { { m i n } }$ using a rapid thermal annealer in air. Further annealing of the final film for $3 0 ~ \mathrm { { m i n } }$ at $6 5 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ with a $1 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } /$ min rate in ambient air resulted in smooth and crack-free films with low surface roughness. The desired film thickness was achieved by repeating the aforementioned coating cycles.

sections.heading: 2.1 | Piezoelectric vibrational energy harvester fabrication
sections.text:
The $\mathrm { L i T a O } _ { 3 }$ piezoelectric cantilevers were fabricated by sputtering Ti $2 0 \mathrm { n m } )$ and Au $\mathrm { 1 0 0 } \mathrm { n m } )$ as electrical top contacts, using a shadow mask, whereas stainless steel substrates served as the bottom electrodes. The specimen size of the piezoelectric cantilever was $1 6 \times 1 . 6 ~ \mathrm { m m } ^ { 2 }$ area and the electrode area was $1 0 \times 1 . 5 \mathrm { m m } ^ { 2 }$ . The samples were named LT-2, LT-4, and LT-6 denoting the coating cycles and subsequently increasing $\mathrm { L i T a O } _ { 3 }$ film thickness.

The crystallinity and phase of the calcined sol-gel films were analyzed by $\mathrm { X }$ -ray diffraction (STOE Stadi MP), using $\mathrm { M o K } _ { \alpha }$ radiation $\langle \lambda = 0 . 7 1 \ \mathrm { n m }$ operated at $5 0 ~ \mathrm { k V }$ and $4 0 ~ \mathrm { m A }$ The surface structure and grain morphology along with the cross-sectional thickness were investigated by scanning electron microscopy (FEI Nova Nano SEM 430). The piezoresponse force microscopy (PFM) was performed using a Bruker Dimension Icon equipped with a $\mathrm { P t / I r }$ coated silicon cantilever (resistivity: $0 . 0 1 0 \mathrm { - } 0 . 0 2 5 \Omega \mathrm { { c m } }$ , spring constant: $3 \ : \mathrm { N } / \mathrm { m }$ , top radius: $2 0 \mathrm { n m }$ ) and a constant AC bias frequency of $5 0 ~ \mathrm { k H z }$ . The ferroelectric and domain switching behavior in the $\mathrm { L i T a O } _ { 3 }$ cantilevers was observed using a piezoforce microscopy technique where the Dual $\mathbf { A C ^ { \mathrm { T M } } }$ Resonant Tracking (DART) mode was used. The dielectric properties were measured using an Agilent E4980A precision LCR meter, and the current-voltage characteristics were recorded by using a Keithley 2400 Source Meter using a home-built 4-point prober. The energy harvesting efficiency was tested using a custom-made shaker setup consisting of a frequency-controlled surface speaker of $2 1 . 2 3 ~ \mathrm { c m } ^ { 2 }$ coupled with an ADXL 343 accelerometer monitored by LeCroy 9350 1 GHz digitizer using a single channel.

sections.heading: 3.1 | Material properties
sections.text: Upon calcination, $\mathrm { L i T a O } _ { 3 }$ film samples showed the formation of a single phase of $\mathrm { L i T a O } _ { 3 }$ perovskite with hexagonal symmetry $( a = 5 . 1 5 \mathrm { ~ \AA ~ }$ and $c = 1 3 . 7 8 \mathrm { ~ \AA ~ }$ as verified by the X-ray diffractogram (Figure 2A). The clear diffraction profile and lack of any unidentified peaks confirmed that no crystalline secondary phases were formed. The SEM images of the $\mathrm { L i T a O } _ { 3 }$ films exhibited smooth and uniform morphology (Figure 2B-D) with uniformly distributed minor cracks possibly formed due to fast shrinkage and the mismatch of thermal coefficient of expansion between the steel substrates and piezoelectric film. No delamination or particle shedding from the cantilevers was observed indicating the well-adherent nature of the films. The cross-sectional SEM images confirmed the film thickness (Figure 2E-G) for samples LT2 $( 2 . 0 7 ~ \mu \mathrm { m } )$ , LT4 $( 3 . 4 1 ~ \mu \mathrm { m } )$ , and LT6 $( 4 . 3 7 ~ \mu \mathrm { m } )$ , respectively.

sections.heading: 3.2 | Effect of poling on the piezoelectric properties
sections.text:
The polycrystalline material has randomly oriented grains or crystallites and has no net domain polarization; however, after the application of high electric field or poling, the material gains a polarizing effect.33 Figure 3A-F presents a typical piezoresponse (PR) phase and amplitude change in the $\mathrm { L i T a O } _ { 3 }$ samples recorded with respect to the increase in film thickness by Vertical PFM (VPFM) and Lateral PFM (LPFM) on an area of $2 \times 2 \mu \mathrm { m } ^ { 2 }$ before and after polarization at $2 0 \mathrm { V }$ The PFM amplitude signal indicates the sample displacement, and PFM phase signal provides information about the polarization vector of individual domains. The appearance of bright or dark regions indicated a difference in the direction of the polarization vector (Figure 3).

![](images/436ca4a058a573e36ae482fb14b7856b3071c93401f0167147cdbb1799e63ed6.jpg)  
FIGU RE 2 (A) 2θ-ω scan of the sample confirmed the formation of single-phase LiTaO $^ { 1 } 3$ (PDF:71-0950), (B-D) scanning electron micrograph of $\mathrm { L i T a O } _ { 3 }$ confirming uniform deposition of thick films [Color figure can be viewed at wileyonlinelibrary.com]

There was no clear contrast present in the VPFM phase before polarization for the LT films as shown in Figure 3A,C,E, which indicated that the out-of-plane domains in the film are largely homogeneous across the entire film possessing early similar domain orientation. The contrast observed at lateral phase mapping in Figure 3C, indicated an arbitrary in-plane domain distribution in case of LT 4 possibly due to an in-plane strain or the surface charge-induced polarization. Further, the spontaneous polarization in the domains was observed by the application of constant DC bias of $2 0 \mathrm { V }$ across LT thin films by the (Atomic Force Microscopy) AFM tip as shown in Figure 3B,D,F, showing a clear modulation in phase between the adjacent domains as analyzed from the dark and bright regions in the LPFM and VPFM phase signals. It was observed that many domains consisted of several grains and some of the grains showed multi-domain structure as well. The piezoelectric properties are supposedly enhanced in the multi-domain state in comparison with the single-domain state due to the strong orientation dependence as well as the extrinsic contribution from the domain wall motions that are asnt  cystasThen plane and in-plane PRs due to the spontaneous polarization of the corresponding domains of the LT film upon $2 0 \mathrm { V }$ bias, as presented in Figure 3B,D,F, also showcase their good ferroelectric and piezoelectric performances. Remarkably, the analysis of LPFM and VPFM images at $2 0 ~ \mathrm { V }$ showed that the in-plane enhancement was higher when compared to the out-of-plane polarization indicating that the response was originated from the polarization of lateral domains aligned perpendicular to the applied electric field. The PFM results confirmed that the LT film possesses strong spontaneous polarization and the polarization switching can be induced at a certain applied voltage.

![](images/ab5b108835853a9596d7393290a4375f71cfe4605aa3b23d084bd49d91f6ca7f.jpg)  
FIG U RE 3 VPFM and LPFM phases and amplitude images of $\mathrm { L i T a O } _ { 3 }$ cantilever surface (lateral scale $2 \times 2 \mu \mathrm { m } ^ { 2 } )$ at different polarization voltages (A): LT-2 at 0 V; (B): LT-2 at $2 0 \mathrm { V }$ ; (C): LT4 at 0 V (D): LT4 at $2 0 \mathrm { V }$ ; (E): LT6 at $_ { 0 \mathrm { ~ V ~ } }$ , and (F): LT6 at $2 0 \mathrm { V }$ [Color figure can be viewed at wileyonlinelibrary.com]

The variations of the PR amplitudes of unpoled LT films and $2 0 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ poled LT films with the DC bias voltage ramped in two directions, exhibit typical "butterfly" loops that are observed in ferroelectric materials. This confirmed the remarkable local microscopic ferroelectric characteristic of the films as shown in Figure 4A,C,E. Further, the ferroelectric domain switching behavior in the $\mathrm { L i T a O } _ { 3 }$ cantilevers was observed from the well-saturated hysteresis loop (Figure 4B,D,F) indicating a $1 8 0 ^ { \circ }$ phase-switching of local domains under the AFM tip. Figure 4, shows the hysteresis and butterfly curve of $\mathrm { L i T a O } _ { 3 }$ before and after $2 0 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ poling for 20 minutes. Figure 4A,C,E, shows the typical butterfly curve and Figure 4B,D,F represents the phase versus electric field strength showing the amplitude under AFM tip that is in contact (tip-on process) with the $\mathrm { L i T a O } _ { 3 }$ surface. It should be noted that due to the dissimilar switching mechanisms among the microscopic PFM and macroscopic P-E measurement, the observed coercive voltage Ec obtained from the PR hysteresis loop is generally smaller than that from the P-E loop as reported for the bulk phase.36 A typical V-shape curve is observed due to the increase in the electrostatic interaction between the cantilever and $\mathrm { L i T a O } _ { 3 }$ samples.37

The converse piezoelectric coefficient $( \mathrm { d } _ { 3 3 } )$ is recognized as an important figure of merit (FOM) for electromechanical applications, such as energy harvesters. The ${ \mathrm { d } } _ { 3 3 }$ coefficient was measured from the slope of piezo PR amplitude (A) versus driving AC bias $( V _ { \mathrm { a c } } )$ according to the equation (may provide graphs and details in Data S1 section):

$$
A = \left( \mathrm { i n v O L S } \right) \mathrm { d } _ { 3 3 } V _ { \mathrm { a c } }
$$

The inverse optical lever sensitivity (inv-OLS), of the AFM cantilever, was determined from the force-distance curve calibrated against a hard reference sapphire substrate (Bruker).

Using Equation (1), the piezoelectric coefficients for the samples LT(2, 4, and 6) were estimated to be 23.23, 21.99, and $2 4 . 0 7 ~ \mathrm { p m / V } .$ , respectively, which were measured at six different points of the sample and averaged over an area of $1 8 \times 1 8 ~ \mathrm { m m } ^ { 2 }$ . These coefficient values match well with the values reported in the literature for polycrystalline $\mathrm { L i T a O } _ { 3 }$ films.18,19

The cantilevers were electrically poled at room temperature at $2 0 ~ \mathrm { V }$ using the PFM tip to enhance the piezoelectric energy output. The hysteresis and butterfly loops revealed the deformation of piezoelectric material under an applied DC voltage. Figure 4C,D showed piezoelectric domain phase versus DC bias voltage representing the local polarization and switching behavior of the $\mathrm { L i T a O } _ { 3 }$ domains.

The net piezoelectric coefficient in ${ \mathrm { d } } _ { 3 3 }$ mode for the $\mathrm { L i T a O } _ { 3 }$ was found to be $2 3 . 2 3 ~ \mathrm { p m / V } .$ at a maximum applied voltage of $2 0 \ \mathrm { V } .$ A typical V-shape curve is observed due to the increase in the electrostatic interaction between the cantilever and $\mathrm { L i T a O } _ { 3 }$ samples.37 From the amplitude, their average roughness was measured to be 19.45, 21.89, and $2 6 . 1 6 \mathrm { n m }$ for LT(2, 4, and 6).

The FOM of a piezoelectric material or a device is applied to provide information about its energy conversion performance. When the material is subjected to mechanical vibrations, the appropriate FOM is given as 38,39:

sections.heading: 3.3 | Dielectric properties and energy harvesting
sections.text:
Figure 5A illustrates the frequency dependence of relative permittivity in the $\mathrm { L i T a O } _ { 3 }$ thin films recorded at room temperature for an applied voltage of $2 \textrm { V }$ amplitude using an LCR meter. At lower frequencies, the relative permittivity was affected by the dipole, interfacial, electronic, and ionic characteristics of the material resulting in higher relative permittivity. However, permittivity starts to lag with the increase in the frequency of applied DC voltage.40 This is due to the space charge effect between the gold electrode and the conductive substrate by which this dielectric trend slows down. Furthermore, these space charge effects are overcome by the applied electric field of $2 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ and the trend saturates above $1 0 0 \mathrm { k H z }$ 41 These trends are similar to other piezoelectric perovskites as well.41-43 At $1 \mathrm { k H z }$ , the relative permittivity recorded was 163.78, 362.20, and 479.73 for samples LT(2, 4, and 6). A lower permittivity value is required to use the device for energy harvesting applications; however, the relative permittivity of these polycrystalline $\mathrm { L i T a O } _ { 3 }$ films is higher than those of single crystal.44 Figure 5B summarizes the leakage current of $\mathrm { L i T a O } _ { 3 }$ cantilevers obtained by applying an electric field of up to $1 2 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ bottom and top electrode of the cantilever, which decreased with film thickness; the resulting current was measured and leakage current density (J) was found to be $4 . 6 5 1 \times 1 0 ^ { - 4 }$ , $4 . 6 5 1 \times 1 0 ^ { - 5 }$ , and $4 . 6 5 1 \times 1 0 ^ { - 7 } \mathrm { A / m } ^ { 2 }$ for the LT samples 2, 4, and 6, respectively, which correlates well with published reports. thicker piezoelectric film has a w leakage current due to different grain size of the material as the number of layers increases.46 A low leakage current ensures efficient charge generation for the piezoelectric applications, as resulting charges dissipate slower.47

The energy output at $1 . 5 \mathrm { m } / \mathrm { s } ^ { 2 }$ acceleration was determined using a $1 \ \mathbf { M } \Omega$ resistor, with $\mathrm { V _ { p - p } }$ of 0.046, 0.104, and $0 . 1 5 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ for LT(2, 4, and 6) (Figure 4C), while the power density was calculated to be 3.99 (LT2), 12.39 (LT4), and $2 0 . 2 3 ~ \mathrm { n W / m } ^ { 3 }$ (LT6). For energy harvesting applications of the piezoelectric material, a high power density is desirable. These results of lower dielectric permittivity, leakage current density indicates free charges on the surface of the cantilevers, accumulated by the dipoles of the $\mathrm { L i T a O } _ { 3 }$ material. These accumulated charges aid to orient the dipoles, resulting in the formation of strong opposition force to the applied electric field.48 The interdependence of the $\mathrm { L i T a O } _ { 3 }$ film thickness and dielectric and piezoelectric properties was comparatively analyzed in Table 1. The results indicated that with increasing film thickness, the roughness of the cantilever surface increases, whereas the FOM was found to decrease. This increase in surface roughness is a consequence of increased resistance to material's ejection,49 whereas due to high relative permittivity, the net FOM decreased with increasing thickness.50 ![](images/69ae7e8a954797bed827eb0750a37112ad79f1f025f97815892928b367bfcb97.jpg) FIU figure can be viewed at wileyonlinelibrary.com] The relative permittivity increased with increasing thickness of $\mathrm { L i T a O } _ { 3 }$ films, whereas the dielectric losses were found to decrease, the reason is the mechanical strain and polarization in the piezoceramic films decrease with increasing film thickness.51 Similarly, the current density decreased with increasing film thickness, whereas a reverse trend was observed for the power density; as with the increasing film thickness, the grain boundary volume also increases, which consequently decreases the net electron mobility in the system due to intergranular charge trapping.52 Figure 6 shows the fabrication conditions to achieve the optimal properties for $\mathrm { L i T a O } _ { 3 }$ cantilevers for energy harvesting applications. Figure 6A shows that the power density decreases, whereas the FOM increases with increasing film thickness. Figure 6B shows the change in relative permittivity and current density with respect to an increase in thickness. A lower permittivity value is desirable to achieve a high FOM, whereas a lower current density is desirable to reduce the leakage of charges within the material. Based on this work, it can be concluded that the thickness of around ${ \sim } 3 ~ \mu \mathrm { m }$ is suitable to achieve the optimum balance between relative permittivity, dielectric losses, and leakage current density.

sections.heading: 3.4 | Repeatability and temperature effect on performance
sections.text:
For a piezoceramic element, its reproducible performance and operability at elevated temperatures are important criteria for device applications. Three sets of cantilevers each of LT2 (LT2-a, LT2-b, and LT2-c), LT4 (LT4-a, LT2-4, and LT4-c), and LT6 (LT6-a, LT6-b, and LT6-c) were tested for repeatability in permittivity, voltage (peak-to-peak), and current density (Figure 7A-C, and Table 2). The cantilevers showed repeatable properties. The standard error for sets of LT2, LT4, and LT 6 was calculated to be in the range of 5.099-9.824 for dielectric permittivity, 0.002-0.007 for peakto-peak voltage, and 0.615-1.961 for current density (Figure 7C, and Table 2). Similarly, the standard deviation for sets of LT2, LT4, and LT 6 was calculated to be in the range of 7.211-13.894 for dielectric permittivity, 0.003-0.010 for peak-to-peak voltage, and 0.87-2.774 for current density (Figure 7D, and Table 2). The results show that an increase in the film thickness (from LT2-LT6) increased the deviation in physical properties possibly due to higher surface roughness and incorporation of impurities during multiple cycles. The effect of temperature on the peak-to-peak voltage generated by $\mathrm { L i T a O } _ { 3 }$ cantilevers was measured, by heat treatment for the samples LT2, LT4, and LT6 for $3 0 ~ \mathrm { { m i n } }$ at 50, 100, and $1 5 0 \mathrm { { } ^ { \circ } C }$ (Figure 7D). It was observed that after each successive heat treatment, a less peak-to-peak voltage was generated possibly due to the increased mobility of ferroelectric domain walls that increased random orientation resulting in depolarization at higher temperatures.53 The depolarization becomes more dominant in a thicker film due to higher grain boundaries within the material and as a result, the higher film thickness increases the change in voltage (measured at $1 5 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } { - } 5 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } $ from 0.012 (LT2), 0.032 (LT4) up to 0.066 (LT6), respectively. However, the net voltage generated in a thicker cantilever is more than their counterpart and is required for MEMS-based VEHs.31 T A BLE 2 Piezoelectric properties of three sets of $\mathrm { L i T a O } _ { 3 }$ cantilever samples

The power density was found to be in the range of $3 . 9 9 { - } 2 0 . 2 3 \times 1 0 ^ { - 9 } \mathrm { W } /$ $\mathrm { m } ^ { 3 }$ increasing with thickness. The permittivity in the range of 163-479.73 was measured at $1 \mathrm { k H z }$ with increasing thickness. The FOM of $\mathrm { L i T a O } _ { 3 }$ cantilevers followed a decreasing trend starting from 3.29 to 1.20 $( 1 0 ^ { - 1 8 } \mathrm m ^ { 2 } / \mathrm V ^ { 2 } )$ . After investigating the abovementioned properties, the optimum film thickness of ${ \sim } 3 ~ \mu \mathrm { m }$ was interpolated to get the highest overall coefficient values for the application of VEHs. The samples were tested at elevated temperatures $( 5 0 - 1 5 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } )$ to determine the depolarization effect. It was confirmed that the samples retained their performance under high-temperature conditions and were also suitable for high-temperature applications. The synthesis, deposition, and fabrication steps were precisely controlled. Moreover, they had great control over temperature and humidity, and the samples were uniform and show great repeatability and reproducibility in their properties which are the need of the hour for VEHs. These $\mathrm { L i T a O } _ { 3 }$ cantilevers are suitable to be integrated into an energy harvester circuit to power up a sensor.

sections.heading: 4 | CONCLUSION
sections.text: Sol-gel technique was successful to deposit thick $\mathrm { L i T a O } _ { 3 }$ films, with thicknesses up to $4 . 3 7 ~ \mu \mathrm { m }$ To our knowledge, it is the highest deposited thickness for this material using the spin coating. In addition, the thickness has been optimized with respect to the other piezoelectric and ferroelectric properties for the application of VEHs. Furthermore, the smoothness, uniformity, and reproducibility of the films were retained. The topography, amplitude, and phase were analyzed of size $2 \times 2 ~ { \mu \mathrm { m } } ^ { 2 }$ area. Investigation of the effect of electrical poling on the piezoelectric properties of $\mathrm { L i T a O } _ { 3 }$ cantilevers showed a clear trend of the orientation of piezoelectric domains by applying an electric potential of $2 0 \mathrm { ~ V ~ }$ .
